newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM asks to exploit business prospects.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM asks to exploit business prospects.

text.p: Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina asked business leaders on Saturday to exploit Bangladesh's improving overseas image, but faced complaints that red tape and weak infrastructure were still blocking trade and investment.
"We no longer suffer from an identity and image crisis. The world now finds a difference between the Bangladesh of today and that of yesterday," she told a meeting with top business leaders in Dhaka.
"Bangladesh has started attracting the attention of the world as an ideal place for trade and investment. My government is free from the stigma of corruption and indecision.
"Exploit the opportunity. You must find avenues and option. You must find (foreign) investors," Hasina said.
But the Prime Minister faced volleys of complaints from the businessmen that bureaucratic tangles and weak infrastructural back-up were holding back opportunities.

"Both foreign and local investors find bureaucratic complexities as one major bar. We appreciate your sincerity for investment but it is not taking root because of red tape," said Yusuf Abdullah Harun, President of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI).
Harun said a company needed permission from 66 different officials to get connected to the electricity net.
He said handling costs in the country's ports were two to three times higher than in other parts of Asia and clearing time was longer.
"How could foreign investment and exports rise in such a state when global competition is going up and up?"

Hasina said her government was trying hard to cut down red tape, and announced that a task force comprising the FBCCI and the customs department would be set up soon to tackle obstacles to foreign trade.
Hasina appealed for "fair business practice and adequate labour welfare" in the private sector.
The prime minister was obliquely referring to a recent crisis in the banking sector over a large number of defaulted loans and fraud in the share market.
An official enquiry last month implicated 36 share brokers and listed companies, including the country's largest corporate house, for manipulating share prices.
Bangladesh's banking sector is grappling with 130 billion taka ($3 billion) worth of defaulted loan.
The business leaders at the meeting said lack of banking support, frequent electricity cuts and congestion in ports had heavily affected industrial output.
Bangladesh currently produces 1,700 megawatts of electricity against a demand of about 2,200 megawatts.

Zafrul Islam Chowdhury, President of the Chittagong Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCCI), said foreign shipping lines were considering declaring the port an "exclusion zone" because of frequent congestion and labour strikes.
The business leaders urged the government to try for a national consensus on major economic issues so that political troubles did not affect industry, trade and exports.
They invited Hasina to sit down with them periodically to discuss problems in trade and industry.
They also called for an immediate brake in tariff liberalisation which, they said, had hit the industrial sector hard.
